target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would broadly remove scheduling barriers and increase turnout
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably give private-sector workers paid time off, so many low-income workers in retail, service, and other jobs could still have to work or lose wages; therefore the holiday may fail to remove the main voting barrier for them and could even worsen it.

target: AG1’s assumption that making Election Day a holiday would, by itself, substantially boost voter turnout
objection: Research says election-day holidays on their own are not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms, so the policy is unlikely to produce meaningful turnout gains without additional measures.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday is a better solution than alternatives such as employer time-off laws or automatic registration
objection: State laws requiring employer time off for voting, or administrative reforms like automatic voter registration, are more reliable ways to increase access because they directly protect time for voting or reduce non-work barriers without depending on holiday compliance.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reduce opportunity-cost barriers for low-income workers by changing scheduling
objection: For many low-income workers, a holiday would not reliably create paid or protected time to vote; if they still must work or lose wages, the holiday can leave their opportunity costs unchanged or higher, so it is not a dependable access improvement.

target: AG1’s assertion that polling places and voter-assistance access would not be systematically less available on a holiday
objection: Many polling locations are schools or community facilities that operate with reduced hours or staffing on holidays, and transportation and voter-assistance services may also be reduced, so voting access could be systematically worse on a holiday than on an ordinary weekday.

target: AG1’s claim that civic celebration and perceived importance of democracy would make a holiday a strong turnout strategy even if some workers still lack paid time off
objection: Even if a holiday raises the symbolic importance of voting, turnout still depends on whether working people actually get time to vote; if they do not reliably get paid or protected time, the symbolic boost is unlikely to generate substantial turnout gains.

target: AG1’s claim that many employers and institutions would close or reduce hours on a federal holiday, making voting easier
objection: Because private employers are not required to give paid holiday leave, low-income workers may still face wage loss or unpaid time, so the holiday does not reliably reduce barriers for the workers most affected by scheduling constraints.

target: AG1’s appeal to OECD countries as evidence that holiday or weekend elections are viable
objection: International examples do not show that a U.S. federal holiday would reliably solve turnout problems, especially when the core issue is whether employers here actually provide paid or protected time and whether the policy outperforms other reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday would reliably translate into more available time and lower opportunity costs for low-income workers
objection: Low-income workers are disproportionately in retail, service, and essential jobs that often continue on holidays, so they may not get the day off; thus the holiday is a less reliable and more distributionally risky way to improve access than enforceable time-off laws or automatic voter registration.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday meaningfully reduces low-income voters’ opportunity costs by freeing daytime schedules
objection: Voting still requires travel, waiting, and completing a ballot, and a holiday can increase same-day turnout enough to create longer lines and more bottlenecks, so the holiday may fail to reduce and can even raise opportunity costs.

target: AG1’s claim that the main cost for low-income voters is missing work or school, so a holiday lowers their net voting burden
objection: The core cost for many low-income voters is not just work/school conflict but also the time spent traveling, waiting, and voting itself; a holiday does not remove those costs, so it does not reliably lower opportunity costs for the group most affected by barriers.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday scheduling would not materially harm polling access
objection: A holiday can increase demand for in-person voting while simultaneously reducing polling-site staffing and facility availability, which can worsen wait times and disrupt access rather than improve it.
